title: How to Argue Effectively Using Philosophy
summary: Effective arguing relies on philosophical logic and disagreeing agreeably rather than simply trying to win. It requires identifying the structure and type of disagreement, steelmanning opposing views, and pursuing truth over persuasion.
key_points: Understand the philosophical structure: An argument consists of premises leading to a conclusion. Determine whether you disagree with the conclusion itself or with the premises and reasoning method used to reach it.

Differentiate validity from truth: According to Aristotelian logic, an argument is 'valid' if the conclusion logically follows from the premises (e.g., 'All cats are philosophers; Socrates is a cat; therefore Socrates is a philosopher'), but the premises themselves can still be completely false.
Practice steelmanning: Formulate the strongest possible version of your opponent's argument before attempting to refute it, even if they cannot articulate it well themselves.
Know both sides: Citing John Stuart Mill's essay 'On Liberty', the creator notes that anyone who knows only their side of a case knows very little about it.
Identify the category of disagreement from three types: facts (what actually happened), explanations (why it happened), or values (what should happen).
Avoid mismatched arguments: If an opponent makes a value-based claim and you respond with statistical facts, the disagreement cannot resolve because you are arguing on completely different planes.

Choose philosophical inquiry over rhetoric: Following Plato's distinction, prioritize philosophical inquiry (discovering what is true) rather than mere rhetoric (the art of persuasion to win an argument).

The most intelligent people are those most able to have constructive arguments!

Transcript:
One of the most important things that you can learn to do well is arguing, but most people are absolutely terrible at it. So here is how to argue effectively according to 2,000 years of philosophy. And if you've ever listened to one of my favorite podcasts, then you will know it pretty much all boils down to this idea of disagreeing agreeably. First, you need to understand what an argument actually is. In philosophy, an argument is a set of premises that lead to a conclusion. So the first thing you need to do is you need to determine whether or not you actually disagree with the conclusion, or whether you disagree with the method and the premises that somebody took in order to get to that conclusion. Aristotle distinguished between different forms of reasoning, and one of the most important concepts in logic is something known as validity. An argument is valid if the conclusion follows from the premises, so the steps that you take to get to that conclusion. But a valid argument doesn't mean that all of those steps are true. For example, let's say all cats are philosophers, Socrates is a cat, therefore, Socrates is a philosopher. That is completely valid logic, but it's completely absurd premises. Socrates is not a cat. So before you even delve into the argument, you need to be thinking about two things. Firstly, do you agree with that person's conclusion? Secondly, do you agree with the premises that lead to that conclusion? And as you take on an argument, you need to do something that is known as steelmanning. This is where you construct the strongest form of the argument that the other person is making and disagree with that. Even if they're not able to articulate that strong form themselves, you are not entertaining this argument simply to be proven right or to look better than the other person. You're entertaining this argument to see whether or not you actually believe the thing that you think you believe. And therefore, you want to be doing the intellectual task of arguing against the strongest possible alternative. In one of his fantastic essays On Liberty, John Stuart Mill argues that somebody who only knows one side of a case knows very, very little of that. The most important thing though that you can be doing is actually identify what sort of disagreement it is that you are having, because if you cannot do this, then you're making an argument out of thin air, there's no point of you having it. There are three very different possibilities generally. First of all, you can disagree about facts, you can disagree about what actually happened. Secondly, you can disagree about explanations, disagreeing about why something happened. And thirdly, you can disagree about values, what should happen. If somebody is making a value-based argument and you are disagreeing with statistics, no amount of back and forth is ever going to resolve it because you are arguing on two completely different planes. And I want to bring you to something that Plato spoke a lot about, and this is the difference between rhetoric, which is the art of persuasion, and philosophical inquiry, which is the aim of understanding what is true. There is a huge difference between going into arguments to win them and going into arguments to discover what is true. You should be airing towards the latter if you really want to be challenging your brain and becoming more intelligent and better at arguments as a whole. Because if you go into every single new argument with the aim of leaving that argument with the same beliefs that you started with, you've completely misunderstood the entire point of arguing. And if you found that interesting, make sure you follow along for more.
